extracted.intended_audience: aviation industry professionals, advertisers, PR/comms teams, and regulatory/compliance officers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and regulatory findings about how airlines may advertise environmental or sustainability attributes of air travel under the UK Advertising Standards Authority (ASA) / CAP Code; focuses on what claims are misleading and what evidence is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Misleading advertising (CAP Code rule 3.1)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ASA argued the advertisements 'gave a misleading impression of the advertiser’s environmental impact' and found that the companies had breached rule 3.1 (Misleading advertising).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statements that create a misleading impression of environmental impact are banned; the rulings stated that the statements 'must not appear again in the form complained about.' The article cites specific ad phrases (e.g., 'Fly more sustainably', 'Air France is committed to protecting the environment: travel better and sustainably') as examples judged misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Environmental claims must be supported by a high level of evidence (CAP Code rules 11.1 and 11.3)
rubrics_metrics.description: The ASA code, written by the Committees of Advertising Practice (CAP), requires environmental claims to be supported by a 'high level of evidence' which would lend proof to the statements made by advertisers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers must be able to substantiate environmental assertions with robust evidence; vague or unproven assertions about sustainability are not acceptable. The article notes the ASA emphasised there were 'currently no initiatives or commercially viable technologies in operation within the aviation industry that would adequately substantiate absolute green claims,' indicating the level of proof required given industry realities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'absolute green' or unequivocal sustainability claims when not substantiated
rubrics_metrics.description: ASA observed that, given aviation's high CO2 and non-CO2 emissions and lack of viable technologies, absolute green statements cannot be adequately substantiated and are therefore misleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not use absolute or blanket claims of being 'green', 'sustainable' or equivalent unless advertisers can produce concrete, industry-relevant, and contemporary evidence that supports those absolute claims. The article implies advertisers should qualify claims or provide clear evidence rather than make unqualified sustainability assertions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedial/compliance action: remove or alter non-compliant adverts
rubrics_metrics.description: The rulings required that the offending statements 'must not appear again in the form complained about' and noted that one airline (Etihad) removed the ad once notified of the complaint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When ASA upholds a complaint, advertisers are expected to withdraw or amend the ad content to remove the misleading claim; prompt removal on notification is cited as appropriate remedial behaviour.
